'''''Luzula campestris''''', commonly known as '''field wood-rush''' or '''Good Friday grass'''  is a [[flowering plant]] in the rush family [[Juncaceae]].<ref name="Stace" /> It is also one of the plants known as '''chimney sweeps'''<ref>{{cite web |title=Field Wood-rush - Luzula campestris |url=https://www.naturespot.org.uk/species/field-wood-rush |website=NatureSpot |access-date=30 March 2024}}</ref>  or '''sweep's broom'''<ref>{{cite web |title=Field wood-rush |url=https://www.wildlifetrusts.org/wildlife-explorer/grasses-sedges-and-rushes/field-wood-rush |website=The Wildlife Trusts |access-date=30 March 2024}}</ref> because of the brush-like appearance of their flowers.<ref name="Grigson">{{cite book |last1=Grigson |first1=Geoffery |title=The Englishman's Flora |date=1975 |publisher=Paladin |isbn=978-0586082096 |pages=542}}</ref> This is a very common plant throughout temperate [[Europe]] extending to the [[Caucasus]]. This species of ''[[Luzula]]'' is found on all types of native [[grassland]]s, and cultivated areas such as lawns, golf-course greens and fields.

==Description==
[[File:Luzula campestris IP0605002.jpg|thumb|Inflorescence]]
''Luzula campestris'' is relatively short, between {{convert|5|and|15|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} tall. It spreads via short [[stolon]]s and also via seed produced in one stemless cluster of flowers together with three to six stemmed clusters of flowers. It is a perennial.<ref name="Stace" />

It flowers between March and June in the northern temperate zone (September to December in the southern hemisphere).  The diploid [[chromosome]] number 2n is 12.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2019|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Fourth|publisher=C & M Floristics|location = Middlewood Green, Suffolk, U.K.| isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>{{rp|987}}
[[Image:Luzula campestris Sturm23.jpg|right|174 px|thumb|''Luzula campestris'']]

It prefers an acidic soil, and when considered a weed in cultivated grass such as lawns, its presence can be readily reduced by decreasing acidity, specifically by removing any accumulation of dead grass material.<ref name="RHS">{{cite web |title=Woodrush in lawns |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/weeds/woodrush-in-lawns |website=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=30 March 2024}}</ref>

==Distribution==
The native range of ''Luzula campestris'' is temperate Europe, extending to North Africa in the south, to the Caucasus in the east and has a northern limit in [[Scandinavia]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Luzula campestris (L.) DC. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:443746-1 |website=Kew Plants of the World On-line |access-date=30 March 2024}}</ref>

''Luzula campestris'' has been introduced worldwide outside its native range into suitable habitats in the southern hemisphere.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/distribution.asp?si=1793|title=Global Invasive Species Database, Luzula campestris }}</ref>

The closely related ''[[Luzula multiflora]]'' is native in much of [[North America]], and is a distinct species in the ''Flora of North America''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200027421|title=Luzula multiflora in Flora of North America @ efloras.org}}</ref> Some botanists treat it as a variety, ''Luzula campestris'' var. ''multiflora''.
